utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not at all important. Maybe it is now important for you at this point, but at that time, it was -- the only thing for me was to save my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously the dates were not important.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I did not prepare myself in terms of remembering the dates. What I concentrated on were the events and my concentration wasn't perhaps all that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the last frame, the 44th minute, please. Let the tape run, please, until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop now. Can we go backwards a bit. Stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this filmed, Mr. Jusic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is my balcony. This is my table, and this is my pear brandy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this filmed after this hit in your apartment and this mess that it caused?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this filmed?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I used a portion of the tape to film my birthday party, and perhaps this remained from that occasion. This was not during the war. This was not during the shooting. I lived alone, and as I do today, and I can see here there are a couple of glasses, perhaps two glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, the frame --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frame --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, the frame showing the gunboat is uninterrupted until this particular frame.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but I told you a minute ago that these gunboats were in the area of Dubrovnik about three or four months and kept opening fire. So it was perhaps one sunny day that I put the table and the glasses outside on my balcony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it could have been after a couple of months?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been after a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: How come this is shown on this tape if, as you told us yesterday, Mr. Jusic, you edited everything that we are viewing here a couple of days after the events, in the cellar of the Libertas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I told you. What I said was that after these - how shall I put it? - the interrogators, the representatives of this distinguished Tribunal came to me, I told them that I was so patriotic as to have a film and to have this footage. They were surprised, and they told me that -- that I should give them this movie, and I had it edited in the TV studio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you edited the film, as you say now, after the visit of the investigators of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And when I went to the television, they took from it the frames showing these direct hits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave the edited material to the investigators of the International Tribunal which you edited according to your selection of material criterion for the material to be seen here today the way we have viewed it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall define it in a different way. What I gave them was the things which were the most important for me, because I'm not a film director, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, you in fact had over your full quarter of an hour. Just understand, we're not unsympathetic to your situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence deeply appreciates your attitude towards us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we thank Ms. McCreath for what she was able to do then. Now Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Kaufman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, just a few more questions by way of re-examination and then you'll be free to go. Now, I'd like to clarify the last matter we raised first of all, about the editing, because I'm still not sure it's clear in all our minds the process of editing that took place with respect to the exhibit that is now currently before the Trial Chamber. That is, the video we've been watching and you've been questioned so much about. You talk about a final process of editing that took place after you received a visit from the Office of the Prosecutor and you had your statement taken from you. Can you explain to us exactly where that editing took place, and when, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, a very serious term is being used here, one that I do not deserve. I'm a composer. I'm not a film director. I did not edit this film, because film editing is a highly responsible job, and this is done by expert individuals. I edited this. There is a video rental store in Dubrovnik that rents videos, that copies videos. It is near the Libertas Hotel. I don't know the exact address. There was a young man there, and he played the tape for me, and I said, "Cut this, keep this," and so on. So I was not there at an editing table, and please try to avoid this particular term "editing," because I'm not a professional. I just wanted to show the suffering of my town. I wanted to show how I could have fallen casualty, my children, my friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, of course I appreciate that, but when I use the word in English, it does not have any particular professional meaning to it. Please understand that. When's your birthday? Perhaps that might assist us. You say that the bottle of brandy was part of your birthday celebrations. When was your birthday that year? On what date? Every year. Sounds like one of those things you always hear about lawyers. When does your birthday fall?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an Aquarius -- I was born on the 26th of January. I'm not going to tell you what year. It's the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those glasses and bottle of brandy would belong to the 26th of January, would they?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Brandy, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about the presence of gunboats around Dubrovnik for a number of months. And I believe it's page 11, line 21 of today's transcript, a wrong date might have been conveyed. The date that was registered was 2002. Now, can you tell us whether those gunboats were around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were gunboats around Dubrovnik already in the summer of 1991. It must have been from August onwards, but they started shooting only later. They positioned themselves there then, and later on they were on the move and they started shooting. This same clip and this gunboat is something that I also took as a way in which they wished me a happy birthday, 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be 2002 or 1992? Just to clarify the mistake that fell in the transcript, page 11, line 21.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could only have been 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let us move back, and we will go in chronological order by way of clarifying some of the matters that were raised in cross-examination. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber and Mr. Petrovic, this matter was raised at page 87, line 2 of yesterday's transcript. You talked about in response to a question from Mr. Petrovic, Dr. Lang sending out a SOS, and you said that it was at 6.00. Was that 6.00 in the morning or 6.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Throughout the film we see you proceeding down the Stradun. As you're proceeding down the Stradun, where is your back facing when you're filming?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you filmed the Maljutka with the threads hanging out lodged in the wall, walking down the Stradun, your back would have still been facing east?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning in response to a question of Mr. Petrovic concerning the music that was coming from Zarkovica when you were conducting Mozart, you said that you heard lyrics and that those lyrics were vulgar. Mr. Petrovic asked you to tell us what those vulgar lyrics were, and I don't believe we got a response, mainly perhaps out of -- for the reason that you felt embarrassed to say those things to the Court. Before I ask you exactly what was said, what was the nature of those vulgarities?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, I have to correct you. Mr. Petrovic said that there was no need for me to provide the text. If you insist, I can tell you, but it's very -- I mean, it is not at the level of this institution. I can write it out for you and hand it over to you and to Mr. Petrovic. I cannot utter those words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you maybe assist us as to the nature of them, the vulgarities, without giving us the exact words that were said by the -- that were being broadcast over these big loudspeakers without embarrassing yourself and going into details?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you will understand what I'm saying, I remembered one verse: "Who does not like a Montenegrin ... his father," if you can catch my drift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't wish to press you on that point. Maybe we better move on in any event. Would you like to write it out, Mr. Jusic, so we can give it to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, what is the point of that, really?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm seeking to find out is whether it was an insult directed at Dubrovnik or just a general insult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the example given --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Your Honour. Maybe I'm just naive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you're searching too hard on a very, very minor issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I shall continue then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about seeing a cannon on Montenegrin TV. Can I show you a photograph, please. If you'd like to look at the monitor in front of you. Sir, what television station is that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is TV Montenegro. This is the hill of Zarkovica, and Dubrovnik is down there. Srdj is on the right-hand side. You can see the fort and then you can see the Elafiti islands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you see a cannon there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an unusual cannon, and if the picture could be moved a bit further up, we would see all of Stradun and all the bell towers that we were discussing this morning. They would all have been hit. So they were probably targeted from this cannon. Also, the Franciscan bell tower and also the one that tells the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to tender that photograph. Because the matter only arose in cross-examination, we're currently having copies of that photograph produced for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. I believe Mr. Petrovic has an objection. So maybe I'll sit down whilst Mr. Petrovic makes his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First of all, it says here TV Montenegro. That is what it says here, but obviously this TV programme was not made by TV Montenegro because you see in the background there is something written in Cyrillic, whereas TV Crna Gora, TV Montenegro, is written in the Latin alphabet. So that is one thing. And the second thing is the following: We would have to know when this footage was made or, rather, when this picture was made. Was it in 1992 or 1995? We cannot tell by this photograph. Therefore, this photograph does not meet the criteria of being admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, do you have anything in respect of its relevance to the 6th of December to submit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's by way of re-examination in response to the matter that was raised about seeing a cannon on television. I wished Mr. Jusic to tell us if this was the sort of thing he'd seen on television. It was an answer given in cross-examination as a result of a question asked by Mr. Petrovic. That's the reason why I'm asking if he recognises the matter. As far as the dating of the photograph is concerned, I'm informed that this is -- forms part of the video that was submitted by Mr. Grbic, which is now a full exhibit before the Trial Chamber. So in essence the matter is already before the Trial Chamber as a tendered exhibit and accepted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see movement to my right. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Yes, very briefly. If it is so, there is no reason for me not to believe my learned friend, but then there is another question that arises that will lead me to ask you for permission to put some questions. This is an 82-millimetre cannon. Is it possible that Mr. Jusic, at a distance of -- a distance of one or two kilometres can see what Mr. Kaufman insinuated just now? So by your leave, I would then put a question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kaufman has been misunderstood by you, Mr. Petrovic. He was saying merely that this was seen by the witness on television, not seen from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If that is so, Your Honour, then there is no problem whatsoever. I do apologise for not having been focused, probably, at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This photograph will be received in evidence on the basis indicated by Mr. Kaufman in his submission a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Copies will be provided in due course, of course, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, does the name Glavac Tasovac mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tasovac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may spell it, it's T-A-S-O-V-A-C.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tasovac. A well-known photographer. An elderly gentleman. His last name is Tasovac but I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about Mr. Pavo Urban's death. Perhaps you might have known about him in reference to Mr. Pavo Urban. If you do, say yes, if you don't, say no.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you were asked about the fact that you had filmed for approximately, or were filming for approximately two hours on the 6th of December yet only a number of minutes appear on the footage that we have in front of us. Do you remember that? And you said and you gave a metaphor or an analogy and said it was -- what you had filmed was like ripping the nail off the finger of a beautiful woman. Sir, that ripping off the nail, was that the sum total of what you saw on that day, or was there more that wasn't captured in the two hours that you were filming?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot more happened that I did not capture in those two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were referring to the nail, we weren't really referring to the legs and arms, we were referring to the burnt down palaces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I used this metaphor, and I believe that a house or a nail is just as valuable as a life, almost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, I'd like to clarify a question that was put to you by Their Honours with respect to the shadows that fell on the Stradun. Now, I'm not sure whether we had a complete answer to that question, so maybe I misunderstood you as well, but I'd like to show you that section of the film again and have you comment on it and tell us whether that shadow that you see in the video, it starts at approximately 18 minutes, is the type of shadow that you would expect for that time of year, namely the 7th of December in the early hours of the morning -- sorry, at the time His Honour put to you, which was at twenty to twelve. If we see the whole section, we will see the point where you also film the clock. We can see the shadows before the clock and after the clock. So these are the shadows before the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I do apologise. It appears we're not broadcasting this. If we could go back, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can stop at this point. It can be seen here that the sun is in the centre, the zenith, and then this here shows that the sun goes through another one of the streets. And then if we go further on, this light will come from the other streets. This is midday, and since it is wintertime, the sun is a bit to the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you just wait there, Mr. Jusic, you will see what happens in a minute, because we get an opportunity to see the shadows once again after you film the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Please, Ms. McCreath, if you could continue the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. This is Nova Street. This is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If you could stop there, please, Ms. McCreath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is the time that is registered there on the clock?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the clock was working on that day, was it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the mechanism. I don't think that the bell tower up there was working, but it is separate. This is a mechanism with Roman numerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Maybe we could just continue slightly a bit further so we can see some shadows afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I wonder if that clarifies the issue for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does, but it raises a question whether the light and shadows shown much earlier in the film when first entering the city are then consistent with what was said to be the time then. There seems some inconsistency between the two, the nature of the light and shadows on those two separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Would Your Honours care for me to explore the issue with the witness? I'm quite able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Entirely up to you, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, Mr. Jusic, at what time you entered the town on that day, the Old Town, on the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 7.00, perhaps a bit before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were filming for how long before your battery ran out?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour and a half or two, approximately. But not continuously. You should be clear on that point. I carried my camera around. I filmed. I would turn it on, I would turn it off, but there are not two hours at a stretch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're talking about an entry around about 7.00, and we have you here filming at 12.00, twenty to twelve or thereabouts. Can you estimate how many times you might have turned the camera on and off during that period and for what period you might have turned the camera off? If it's difficult for you to remember, say, "It's difficult for me to remember."

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rewind the tape so that we can see when I'm entering town and when I'm approaching the main street, Stradun?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. It can be found at approximately 13:30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we actually do see a bit of sunlight here, so perhaps we could stop here, Ms. McCreath. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the sunlight falling there. Are you aware, through your familiarity with the Old Town, at what time of day the sun falls on that part -- the sun's rays fall on that part?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 6.30 and 7.00. You can see that the sun is coming from the east, and the upper parts are lit. So you can basically see this line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the pattern of sun rays falling that you would expect to see at that time of day, is it, sir, at that month of the year?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, the point of concern was the scene shown when first entering the Stradun when there was comment on the large number of people that were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Petrovic could remind me as to the exact time. I believe it's somewhere around the 14 minute mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour. Fifteen minutes, 30 seconds, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you could stop, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, sir, take a look at the tower at the bottom, first of all, before we talk about shadows. Do you see the Red Cross flag on the tower there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what -- you also talked about an air raid siren going on. Do you remember at what time the air raid siren went on that day? The 7th of December. This is the day you said there was an air raid siren.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The siren was on the previous day, around 6.00. And then it was on until about 9.00 in the morning. That's why these people are here. They were people trying to extinguish the fires. Then around 9.00 again the siren went off, and then again we can see that these people can no longer be seen in the remaining footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would this be -- before we talk about the shadows, would this be before the siren went off again or after the siren went off again? Just so it's clear for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just before the siren went off. But I would like to draw your attention to another thing. You can see the sun from the east, the first sun rays in the morning, on the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was going to come to now, sir, because we're talking from your last answer, without, of course, leading you on the matter, I understand this is -- would have to be before 9.00. So looking at the sun rays as they fall on the buildings going down the Stradun, would that be the type of sun ray pattern you would expect to find, being a resident of Dubrovnik and familiar with the Old Town, in the month of December before 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the morning hours in Dubrovnik, the time that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you aware of stopping your camera at a time after 9.00 in the morning and then turning it on later? Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you play this a bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At this point I stopped filming, the next second or so. This was the -- this is when I took the battery here to the right, to our city hall, to recharge it. And this is already midday when I set out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have a gap, if this is already midday, as you say in your last answer, from -- of approximately three hours. Am I correct? If the first image was --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. From 9.00 to twenty to twelve. Approximately from 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it yourself that this is the same day? Just so it's clear for the Court and for all concerned, and for Mr. Petrovic especially.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, without any dilemma whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an explanation? If you know, just say, "I know"; if you don't, just say, "I don't know," why the Red Cross flag was -- seems to be shown on the same building where it isn't shown early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably hit by something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave it at that. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Kaufman, while the -- Mr. Jusic's mind is on these matters, the earlier filming, as you first came into Stradun, you've indicated just then it was before, perhaps, 9.00. I think earlier you said you went into the city to film at around 7.00 in the morning. Are you able to say what time it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I didn't quite articulate it properly. I shall repeat. I set out going into the city before 7.00 and then started filming around 9.00, and then I went to recharge the battery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the first filming was not at 7.00 but around 9.00. Is that what you're now saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. The first filming was around 7.00. This is when the sun rises in Dubrovnik. The sun rises between 6.30 and 7.00. So actually it was at 7.00 or before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last question, and this is on a totally different matter entirely. You were shown the refectory of the Franciscan Monastery. You were asked how you could explain that the pitcher of water was intact. Do you know when the pitcher of water was placed there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, I thank you very much for your coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if the Trial Chamber has any further questions of this witness that I haven't covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. Mr. Jusic, I'm pleased to be able to tell you your time here is at an end. May we thank you for your coming and the time you've spent here and your assistance, and you are now free to return to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, just a couple of words. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm deeply honoured to have been acquainted with this august company. I am deeply privileged to have come here to present the truth. I'm grateful to the colleagues who conducted this discussion with dignity, and I have to say to Mr. Strugar that none of this should have happened. We could have lived in peace as good neighbours, and it is indeed a pity that what happened did happen. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now do I turn to -- Ms. Somers. There are three wise heads there. I didn't know to which to turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are prepared to present the next witness, Mr. Vlasica, if the Chamber would permit us to go directly in. As -- with respect to the submissions on the documentation that came up in exhibit last week, I would indicate to the Chamber that in order to clarify some of the points that were brought to my attention of being of concern, we are endeavouring to contact the institute to see if it could be clarified further from persons from the institute. There will be additional evidence led that will cover damage unless -- if the Chamber is minded to permit the evidence to come in before any further legal submissions need to be heard, I only suggest that perhaps it might be helpful. It is entirely within, obviously, the Chamber's discretion, but we will move with more evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be more practical and perhaps in the end speedier if we deferred then the question of the admissibility of that document until we see what is the totality of the evidence. I think that would suit your position, wouldn't it, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is neutral vis-a-vis our position. However, there is another circumstance which has to be taken into consideration. If some new material is going to appear, and of course in all these matters we are talking about hundreds of pages, Your Honour, I am afraid that we shall perhaps not be able of efficiently and quickly operating with hundreds or thousands of pages which will be produced in the middle of this trial in an exercise which is by its very nature formidable. So I just wish to point out the skepticism and apprehension on the part of the Defence to the effect that we'll be able to competently render our opinions and judgements in relation to this new material. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Mr. Petrovic. I can say these things: From what I understand, what is foreshadowed is the calling of one or more of the people actually involved in the preparation of the report as to damage. You've already dealt with two witnesses of that nature. If it should be that the Prosecution does suggest more evidence of that type, it will be possible then to assess whether the task of absorbing it would be within your capacity without some adjournment or whether some adjournment will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I just want to make it clear that if one of these individuals is available, and I'm hopeful, that there should exist statements from one or both of those persons, and the time frame, I believe, would be fairly quick. And further, it's not because we feel there is any change in admissibility, per se, but we would like at least to have the benefit. Our position, of course, is that it is admissible, but, rather, we want to make sure the Chamber has as good a record as possible, and we appreciate the deferral. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the issue then of the legal admissibility will be deferred, and you now offer us a new witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We'll try very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, a clarification which I believe is appropriate. Of course, without any pretensions on the part of the Defence to judge what the Prosecution wishes to present before this Trial Chamber and in what way, Your Honour, at this point the legal situation is such that the admission of this Exhibit P51 was requested through the witness Colin Kaiser. I would therefore be grateful if Madam Somers would withdraw that motion and then proceed in whatever way she feels is expedient. So we have this request by Mr. Kaiser. So this should be an exhibit in connection with the testimony given here by Mr. Kaiser. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Mr. Petrovic, but I really don't think it's necessary to pin the exhibit down at the moment to a particular witness. We already have more than one witness speaking to its content, and it is possible now that we will have one or more further witnesses. I think we'll wait until we see what the body of evidence about the document is, and then we will hear both Prosecution and Defence as to whether it should properly be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I continue to look at the three wise heads wondering which it is that I'm to here next. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, whilst the witness is being brought in perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: -- I'd like to tender the exhibit that was presented in re-examination, P83. That's just for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to take the affirmation from the card that is to be handed to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Ivo Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I'm 46 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: At Mokosica, which is a suburb of Dubrovnik. The address is Izmedju Dolaca number 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I have two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you employed, or what do you do for work?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I'm a shopkeeper. I own a store, a shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is this store?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It is at Mlini.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that within the Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: That is the Zupa Dubrovacka. This is another municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you also a pensioner, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you receive any pension from the Croatian government as a result of injuries you suffered?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you ever serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you serve full time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: From 1978 to 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Sabotage Reconnaissance Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any special training in that unit?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long of a training course did you have to take?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Seven months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was your rank when you left the full-time military in 1979?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: A squad leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you left, did you become a reservist?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year were you in the reserves?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you completed your military service in 1989, what if any rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I was a reserve Second Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever join any other political party after being a member of the communists?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you completed your military service, did you attend any additional schooling?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. I attended a school in order to obtain additional training for my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you completed your school, what did you do for work?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I was the foreman. I -- I ran a store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of this store?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It was the work organisation called Dubrovkinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located, your store?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It was in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what street?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Ulica Od Puca, the Od Puca Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said it was part of a work organisation. What do you mean by that? When you say "Dubrovkinja," do you mean it's part of a chain or a franchise; what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Well, it was one of a chain of stores, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of stores? What did you sell?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Foodstuffs, bread, milk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you -- or let's move to October 1, 1991. Can you tell us where you were at about 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: At 6.00 in the morning, I was going to work, and I was near the fire brigade above the Old Town. I was in my car, going to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen? Did you observe something at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I could see to my left that shelling had started someplace from the Srdj slope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I went to the parking lot at Buza, and I left my car there, and I rushed into town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the shelling continue?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The shelling continued, as far as I was able to hear, because I was already at Uzine by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is Uzine?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The walls are around Dubrovnik, so the fortress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go to -- let's take it a step back. Did you go to your store first?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay -- how long did you stay at your store?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: For eight hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to a shelter that date?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the shelter, inside or outside of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Inside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which shelter did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I went to the shelter at the aquarium in the St. John Fort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's discuss the situation in Dubrovnik, especially the Old Town, in October, November, early December 1991. What was the status of the power or electricity?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It was bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "it was bad"? Was it functional? Was it --

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? What happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: As there had been shelling by the JNA at Komolac, the electricity went down in the Old City automatically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the lack of power affect the water supply?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: As the electricity is the only thing which propelled the generators, the turbines in Komolac, this automatically means that the water supply was cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any blockade around the city of Dubrovnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was blockading the city?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was with its ships from the sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about on the land?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: On the land, their forces were advancing towards Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the blockade, did that affect the ability to import food into the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there refugees in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Many. Many. Plenty of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: From Konavle, from Zupa, from Osojnik, from all the surrounding places around the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the many refugees and the blockade -- with the many refugees and the blockade, was there sufficient food in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we need a break at this time or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your last -- in your last answer, you indicated there wasn't sufficient food in the Old Town. Were all the grocery stores in the Old Town still operational?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your store open for business?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any private stores, smaller private stores open for business?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: There was one in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the stores?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The others were closed because the people were afraid that they would get killed when they came to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have product to sell?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: There were goods inside the stores, and we transferred them from store to store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did your store, Dubrovkinja, remain open?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Because I, as a young man, had my car, and I volunteered, in fact, to work there. I was able to come quite quickly to town from Lapad, and perhaps I was not as afraid as the other people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they have food to sell?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In the shops you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in your shop.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there sufficient bread in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how -- why was it that there was sufficient bread in the Old Town during this period?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Because the Orlando bakery worked during the night, and then during the night we would get the bread that they had baked. It was transported to the Old Town by trucks while it was still dark so that the JNA would not discover the trucks and not shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you become a member of the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what month?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The Civil Defence is a way of helping civilians in terms of food, medicine, accommodation, shelter, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it associated in any manner with the military?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Civil Defence members wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry guns?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your store associated with the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I was within Dubrovkinja, and that was the store that was supposed to be involved in supplying the town with proper supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What hours were you opened for business to supply the town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: From 6.00 a.m. until 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "8.00," do you mean 8.00 in the morning or 8.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: 8.00 in the morning. If it were in the evening, I would have said 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Why was the store only open for two hours?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In terms of safety measures, we were supposed to distribute the food we had as soon as possible so that we could go back to the shelters, because we never knew whether there would be shelling and when it would be take place. At first we were sure that there would be no shelling of the Old Town, but what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue in October. Were any efforts made to protect any of the culturally important buildings in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Civilians, people from work organisations who were within the big construction company and so on, we took construction material, wooden boards, and we protected cultural monuments, because we had received information that there might be an attack on the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give us an example of some of the buildings or objects that were protected?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Viewed from St. Blaise, Orlando's pillar, the Gundulic monument, then the palaces, then the facades of all churches, because facades are very important, and the reliefs there. So everything that had to do with old monuments, and the two fountains as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any large flags flying over the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, the UNICEF flag and the Red Cross flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean UNICEF or UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: UNESCO, UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the Old Town -- I'm sorry. Where were the flags flying? Let's start off with the UNESCO flags. Where were they flying?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The UNESCO flag was on Fort Minceta, on St. John's Fort. Yes, those two forts, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Red Cross flags?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: On Fort Revelin and St. John's Fort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were Fort Revelin and St. John's Fort being used?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: They were used as shelters for civilians from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October of 1991, was the Old Town shelled?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to November. Where were you working in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Also at the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you still just working in the mornings?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your wife and children? Did something happen to them in November?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: My wife worked at Lapad, at Cokolino, which was also within Dubrovkinja, until the 5th of November when a large-scale attack took place against Lapad. I was afraid for her and for my children, so on the morning of the 7th, I sent them out of Dubrovnik by ship, because the Yugoslav army was only allowing women and children to leave town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in the municipality of Dubrovnik after they left on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: At Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of house was it that you were living in?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I lived as a sub-lessee at the apartment of the Karaman family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were living in the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In that house was our landlady, her daughter-in-law, and 22 other people, including us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had those other 22 always lived there?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were they from?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: From Zupa and Konavle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any refugees living in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had they moved into hotels within the Old Town or were they living with friends or relatives?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: With friends and relatives, in their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in November, where were the JNA forces located?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In November, the JNA forces were on the slopes of the hill of Srdj at Komolac and Mokosica, and the entire area in the direction of Split, all the way up to Slano, I think. That is to say that we were totally surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any forces on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe on Zarkovica in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Since we had no water and since we had to operate the way we did at the store, we had to bring water from the sea in order to use it in the store when we went to the toilet. So then I went carrying jerry cans in order to bring seawater and then I saw trucks and men at Zarkovica belonging to the JNA. That can be seen quite well from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have, then, a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before the break, you mentioned that you had seen trucks and vehicles on Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Or you observed forces. Did you observe anything other than forces on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you able to observe anything on Strincera?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: On Strincera I noticed a Yugoslav tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to hear any sort of singing or songs from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I heard their own authentic music.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "authentic music," are you talking about nationalistic songs?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Not at that moment, although I know that they sang that, too, because I heard about it from other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear the nationalistic songs?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. The witness, in response to my learned colleague's question, gave two answers; that he heard authentic songs. That is one answer. My colleague Mr. Weiner then asked him whether they were nationalist songs, and the witness decidedly said that he did not hear any nationalist songs, but he said that he heard that other people were talking about that. Now my colleague Mr. Weiner asked him, "When did you hear nationalist songs?" So he is putting words into his mouth. He did not say that. He had not said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at line 13 of the transcript, he said not at that moment. So my response is I was going to ask him -- or I did ask him when did he hear it if he didn't hear it at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there's some validity in what Mr. Rodic is saying, Mr. Weiner, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear any type of songs, sir, coming from the mountain?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I myself did not hear that, but I heard from my friends that they heard that when they went to Porporela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was the city shelled in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it heavier? Was the shelling heavier than in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the dates that the city was shelled, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Since the total blockade came into place between the 7th and 12th of November, during those three or four days there was an incredible amount of shelling of the Old Town itself and the town beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shelling in Old Town's harbour?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, happened to the boats in that harbour?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is what happened to the boats?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The small passenger boats that transported people to the islet of Lokrum were destroyed then, and also an old boat. I can't remember its exact name now. It had been hit, too, and it sank. I don't know exactly how many, but a great many fishermens' boats belonging to civilians were sunk and hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your car in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: During the shelling of Babin Kuk, because the Yugoslav army constantly targeted the area of the hotels at Babin Kuk where civilians were, so they targeted them all the time, and during this shooting, as this shooting was going on, shells were falling on Babin Kuk where I lived, and that's when my -- that's when my car was hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after your car was hit in November or -- or first let's step back. Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your car was destroyed, did you continue to go to work in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. In the early morning hours, while it was still dark, I went on foot from Babin Kuk to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to December, December 6th. What did you do that morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: On the morning of the 6th, early in the morning, I came to the store because that morning I was supposed to distribute a large amount of bread. I had set out from Babin Kuk from 5.00 in the morning, so at 6.00 I had arrived in Boninovo. Then I saw on my left-hand side the hill of Srdj, and I saw that large-scale shelling had started and a great deal of shooting. I expected something big to happen, but I thought I will go on because I was supposed to distribute bread that morning. I passed by the hospital. I entered the Old Town and came to the store. I prepared a cup of coffee, and I turned on the radio. The morning news on the radio were a bit late, and they said that a large-scale attack was expected on Dubrovnik and that big JNA forces were on their way. I did not know exactly whether the Old Town would be attacked, so then I stayed on in the store. When the first shell fell - this was sometime between 6.30 and 7.00 - I thought to myself, "Ivo, this is no good." At that moment, the late Skocko passed by in a type of vehicle that was used in the Old Town for transporting food supplies. It actually -- it is actually a battery-operated vehicle, and it is used for delivering supplies. As he was transferring bread to his shop, Kate Buric, an employee of mine, came to me and said, "Boss, I don't know whether we'll be getting any bread this morning. I would like to go and get some bread from Skocko." I said, "Kate, go but come back soon and then we'll see what we'll do." She went there and came back, and at that moment, perhaps a few minutes later, I felt as if a truck was coming, and I said, "Kate, the bread is coming." I went out to the doorstep of the store and I stepped outside with my right foot. I looked in the direction of the Rector's Palace. On my left-hand side I realised it was not our truck, rather, at that moment, somebody had taken Skocko's truck towards Gospa. At that moment I felt the detonation of a shell, and I received an exit/entry wound on my right foot. I turned around and I said, "Kate, I've been wounded." I walked back two steps and I lay on the floor. The exit/entry wound was on my right side, and I did not know at that point whether it was an exit wound as well, because being so afraid as to what would happen to me, I just saw the entry wound. I lay on the floor, and she tried to stop the bleeding because a lot of blood was coming out of the wound. After awhile, we noticed that blood was curdling in my trousers. Then we realised that the exit wound was even bigger than the entry wound. She called the doctor who was at St. John's Fort and at Revelin. I don't know exactly which doctor she received this information from, that, of course, she should not put anything on the wound and that if she had anything, she should try to bandage the wound and stop the bleeding. Since the shelling of the Old Town itself was incredibly intense, an ambulance could not come. Nobody could enter town due to fear and, of course, because of the shelling itself. So I lay there for two hours, bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just stop there for a second. You said at first you were shot in the foot. Where were you shot, sir? You said the right foot. Were you shot in the foot?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Not in the foot but in the right upper leg, between the knee and this part here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that shortly. So in the right upper leg. Do you mean the thigh?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you said after you laid down, you said Kate tried to stop the bleeding. What did she do the first time when she tried to stop the bleeding?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. As I was wearing jeans and had a jeans jacket and I also had jeans on my legs, she used my belt, tightening it just below the thigh in order to staunch the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that work?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Actually, no, it didn't, because the entry wound was quite large. She was not successful, but the bleeding was less profuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that she then called a doctor who said try anything to -- find something to use as a bandage. What -- what did she wind up doing?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: As I was quite frightened seeing that the situation was like that, that I was bleeding and my blood pressure was automatically dropping, and of course in addition to that I was afraid of a shell landing directly on us because there is nothing -- there was nothing above me, there was no concrete slab, there was nothing which was made of solid material but something which was made of wattle, I believe. It was lightweight material which was above us. So I was afraid that a shell might land directly on me. So in this situation she, too, was afraid and feared for her life, so she called the doctor, asking him what we were to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the doctor told her use anything you can to bandage it, what did she use? What did she do to bandage your leg? Tell us how she did it.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In our shop we didn't have anything but two or three crates of lemon, and we had some tampons, ladies' tampons, so this is what she used at that particular moment. She used Kotex, the pads, and she tore my shirt and wrapped my wound with it, and that helped as much as it could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Very, very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she able to give you anything? Was there any coffee? Was there anything she could give you at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: As I said, there was nothing in the shop apart from lemon. She squeezed some lemon juice, and as the doctor said, don't let him fall asleep, because if he does, he will die on you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you were there for some hours because you couldn't get an ambulance. Did the shelling continue during that morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how extensive or heavy or light was the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It was very extensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to get an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No. No, we weren't. Actually, sometime around 9.30 - I cannot recall the exact time - of course given the situation I was in at that particular moment, I don't see how anyone could remember the exact time. Anyway, she got in touch with the people in the office at Dubrovkinja and fortunately, the telephone lines were functional. So she told them down there, "Ivo has been wounded. What are we to do? He can die." So between those -- of these people, I did not know exactly this person, but later I found out who was the person who had saved my life. So Mr. Mario Mrkusic, who was one of these people, took his yellow Golf car and was courageous enough and responsible enough to take this yellow Golf of his and set out from the old barracks, which is at Lapad, and came and fetched me, and I was already at the end of my strength. So he took me and Kate, and then we took the Od Puca Street directly to the Pile Gate. As we were going through the Od Puca Street, I noticed a fire, a blaze to my left, meaning that I saw houses that were burning, houses which were opposite the Orthodox church. There was an incredible amount of material on the street so that he had to dodge the rubble, the bricks, all the debris on the floor, on the pavement, rather. And I remember only that we arrived eventually at Pile, the Pile Gate. The Hotel Imperijal was also on fire. It was ablaze, and that's all I remember. I don't recall anything else because at that moment I fainted, and I only came to at the hospital. And the hospital is in the new part of Lapad, and this is a new hospital, by the way, because the orthopaedic ward and the surgical ward, all these medical - how shall I put it? - the medical and surgical ward had already been transferred to this new hospital and were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just step back. Now, you said one of the people or one of those persons was this gentleman who came over and helped you, Mr. Mrkusic. Was he an employee of Dubrovkinja?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he an employee at the administrative officers where Kate called?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw some damage as you were leaving. You indicated three buildings opposite the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any other damage that you saw before you left through the Pile Gate?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I saw the Onofrio fountain. It had been hit. And also in Siroka Street I noticed a house on fire. Basically, I noticed a lot, but believe me, at that particular moment, with my life endangered, I was not paying so much attention to what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, could he please stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that may be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlasica, could you please stand up for a moment and step to the side so the Court could see. Could you step to the side. To the right -- or left side. Thank you. Could you please first show the Court how you were standing in that entryway. You said you were standing partially out the entryway of your store when you got hit.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: This is the door, this is the street, so I went out in this fashion and looked downwards. At that moment, a shell landed to my right, and I was hit here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First, may the record reflect that the witness is standing at an angle, with his right foot out front at kind of a 45-degree angle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now show once again on your leg where the entry wound was, please. Show the Court.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness is pointing to his right leg, approximately ten to 15 centimetres below the hip. By the pocket, the right side pocket.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. By the right side pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And on the outer aspect of the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, on the outer side of the leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please turn and show the Court where the exit wound was, if you could, as best you could.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: [Indicates]?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect, Your Honour, that he is pointing to the inner thigh, the upper part of it, approximately 20 centimetres above the knee. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. You can sit down again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 13. Actually, could we show him this copy of Exhibit 13 in case he'd like to mark. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise that map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put an X where you worked, using one of the pens or pencils, to show the Court where you worked.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you just point to the Court -- could you show them the area where you saw Tonci Skocko pass on that kind of trolley, that little truck or however you want to describe it.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Taking the Od Puca Street towards my shop, which is here in -- I believe that the name of the street is Uska Street. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness, using the pointer, pointed down Od Puca Street from the beginning with Lucarica Street, pointing towards the intersection of Od Puca Street and Uska Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple questions about Mr. Skocko. You said the late Skocko. Which Skocko are you referring to? Do you know the man's first name?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Skocko Junior, the son, Tonci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw Tonci Skocko drive by in that small truck with bread on it, can you tell us, do you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in a uniform of some kind, whether a work uniform or a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a gun or a weapon? Did you see a gun or a weapon on him?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did for work, Tonci Skocko?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: He helped his father in his father's shop, being his son of course, and that was a family business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his father's shop, was that one of the private grocery stores?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes. It had a wide assortment of goods. There were fruits, there were vegetables, all sorts of foodstuffs, detergents, beverages; sort of a supermarket store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, looking at the map, could you please show us the route that you drove to leave the Old Town and go towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: So from the spot of wounding, taking the Od Puca Street, so from the place where I was wounded, through the Od Puca Street, up to the exit towards the Pile Gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were leaving, you said that you saw some houses that were on fire. Can you give us an idea of the area where the houses were, approximate area?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Well, as for the exact location, yes, it's here. Number 21. I believe this is where the Orthodox church should be on this map. And opposite from number 21, towards me, was the place where these houses were on fire. And there was the barbershop of Jako, a well-known barber, there. And here also was a shop, the Yugoslav shop, which also burnt down. So it is in this row here of houses opposite from the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you also show us the area that you said that you saw rubble -- or, no, you said that you saw material on the street and that they had to dodge that to get you out of there.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
