utterances.text: Mr. Mrkusic, who was driving me, he had to evade the fragments and stone pieces and shards and the pieces of the building material that had fallen on the street. So this entire street -- in this entire street that we took, everything was on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say the entire street, are you referring to Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And one last thing on that map. Could you please show us the -- you said the fountain was damaged. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness is pointing to number 5 on the map. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you fainted. When did you awaken or regain consciousness? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I was on a table in the hospital. They were going to X-ray my leg because they wanted to determine whether the bone was fractured. And as they were ripping off the clothes off me, I regained consciousness at that particular moment, and the only thing I did was to ask the person who was attending to me whether my bone was damaged, and he said, "No, Ivo, it isn't." And believe me, I was relieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I remained there from the 6th to the 21st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, did you receive any blood?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you lost much blood from the wound?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know how much blood I had lost, but I did bleed profusely. And to illustrate this, as I said at the beginning, there was a blood clot, and that meant that a lot of blood had actually left my body. Not being a doctor, I don't know exactly how much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you got to the hospital on that day, did they stitch or suture the wound immediately? Did they stitch it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No, they didn't. There was a big gap, and the entry wound was quite large, and as this was caused by shrapnel, of course it had to be cleaned to avoid the wound from being contaminated and infected, because that could mean that my leg would have to go off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they eventually stitch the wound?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did. I don't know when exactly, how much time had passed, but they did suture the wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who stitched the wound, a doctor or a nurse or -- who stitched it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: While they were stitching the wound, they moved me from the cellar, from the basement to the suture room and the room in which they perform surgery, and it was Dr. Dalmatin who did the stitching with the aid of two nurses, two anaesthesiologists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they stitched your wound, did you they use any anaesthesia?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Since the wound was not that large, it was -- no, they didn't use any anaesthesia on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wasn't anaesthesia used? Was there a large amount of anaesthesia in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Well, from what I heard from the nurses, they didn't have anaesthetics in abundant supply there so that, in minor cases, this was the procedure applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the nurses did to enable the doctor to stitch or suture your leg?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: One of the nurses held me -- held my chest and the other held my legs, held down my legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did she hold down your hands? Did any of them get on top of you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: She lay on me. She had to in order to actually hold me down in the bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they put anything in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, some gauze in order for me not to bite my tongue or do any harm to my teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as these two nurses held you down, did the doctor stitch your leg?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: It wasn't the proper suturing procedure. It wasn't a regular suture. On the upper side there were three, and on the lower side there were four, and there was an interval in the centre because the wound promised to heal very quickly. So they just wanted to put together the upper and lower parts of it. I can show you. I can show you how actually the actual suturing was done. It is still obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you in pain during this suturing or during this stitching? Did it hurt?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Of course it hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in the hospital for approximately 15 days, a little over two weeks.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you left the hospital, did you have to return for out-patient treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. I would come every day to the hospital for dressing, for my wound to be dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say your wound had to be dressed, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: First they would clean the wound and then they would apply a new bandage. As I couldn't remain in hospital nor were there any beds in fact in the hospital at the time because of the large number of wounded and there were wounded people all over the hospital, it was only natural that we with minor wounds would be discharged. So we went home, but we did return repeatedly in order to be examined for any contamination or sepsis and, God forbid, gangrene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say you were in a room, you were in a room with other patients during the 15 days you were in hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know in your statement you mention that you became friends with another patient called Zika. Is that the proper pronunciation of his name?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, this Zika I can say was one of the most courageous people up on the hill of Srdj. When the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army came quite close, practically at the very entrance to the fort, a shell landed near him, and I don't know exactly from which side, he didn't tell me that, actually it was a hand grenade and wounded him, and he was dead, 80 per cent dead. I mean, with the help of Sveto Antunovic who carried him down - and he is of a slender build, this Zika - so this person carried him down to the coastal road below the Srdj, and from there they took him to the hospital, and he told me how bloody it had been up there. And he also told me, "Believe me, if we were not that courageous, they would have killed us all."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Zika who was with you in the hospital who you described as courageous, what was the nature and extent of his injuries?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: He had very many wounds. As I said in my statement, literally speaking, he was 80 per cent dead. He couldn't pass stool, he couldn't have any normal functions. Everything, all of these functions were actually led outside his body through a portion of his stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you talk about your injuries being not as serious, you're comparing that to his or other people in that category, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got out of the hospital after 15 days, you testified that you went for out-patient treatment. How long -- how long did the pain last in your leg?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I felt this pain in my leg for a good 40 days, until it had more or less wholly healed and I could be able to walk. I had to walk, in fact, because I had no one to escort me, I had no car, so I had to exercise my muscle which had been pierced. But still today I feel the pain, especially when there are weather changes. Of course I can feel my leg reacting to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- so over 13 years later, you still feel pain in that leg, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, even today. And even today, a partly damaged part can be seen which covers a large surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you a document from the hospital to look at, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, or Your Honours, this witness, when he arrived, brought this document, and we're having it interpreted at this time. So -- and we've given it to the interpreters. If you'd like to have them read it, or I could have this witness read it. All right. Why don't we start off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They did get it yesterday. Much faster than I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I got this document from the hospital before I came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that document and what does it concern?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: This is my discharge sheet from the hospital confirming that I had been wounded and that I was in hospital between the 6th and the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the names of the persons who signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is currently the director of the hospital in Dubrovnik, and Dr. Jaksa Segedin, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you read it, the B/C/S version, into the record, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no need for us to waste time, because we have got the document both in B/C/S and in English. So I believe it is superfluous for it to be read out. The witness explained what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As most times, Mr. Rodic, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I'll offer it at this time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, may I address you? If this document is being admitted into evidence as a Prosecution Exhibit, the Defence kindly asks that it only be marked for identification now because we received the document only yesterday. So then after cross-examination a final decision can be made on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From -- from the translation, Mr. Weiner, it seems to be describing an injury to the other leg than the one identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but it's on their left and his right. Looking at him it's on the left, and -- if you look at a person it's their left and on that person itself it's his right. What angle or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you any problem with the document as it is one that hasn't been considered by the Defence being simply marked for the moment until they've had a chance to consider it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fair. That's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P84.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you got out of the hospital and completed your out-patient treatment, did you ever return to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: In February 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned, did you walk through the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what areas of the Old Town did you walk through? Could you show them on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Across Stradun, along Lucarica Street, then Gunduliceva Polja, then my street, Od Puca, where I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you notice? Let's start off on Stradun that you just showed us where you walked. What did you notice on the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: A great deal of destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at destruction at a range from shrapnel damaging a facade to total destruction of a building, totally destroying a building, how many buildings in the Stradun received some sort of damage?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: I don't know if there was one that had not been damaged. Basically every one of them had been hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this condition or level of damage to all the buildings on the Stradun, did this exist prior to December 6, 1991? Was it in that condition prior to December 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you walked along Od Puca Street, your street where your store was. What did you observe along Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: Since two months had gone by since I had last been in town, of course it was cleaned so that the town could function properly. All the debris that had fallen on the streets had been cleared and the damage was due to the shelling. However, the town of Dubrovnik was gravely wounded. One could see what had burned down and also one could see a great deal of damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about Od Puca Street. Could you describe, as best that you can recall, the damage that you saw in February 1992 on Street Od Puca after you returned?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: How can I put this to you? When you imagine the house that was on my left-hand side, it was intact before and now you can see that it had burned completely, from top to bottom. Only the outside walls were left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting my learned friend once again, but I believe that this is relevant in view of the period of the indictment. That should be borne in mind when speaking of the damage. The question of the damage that could be seen in February 1992, specifically this is a point in time which is three months after what had occurred on the 6th of December. What happened in the meantime is not clear. What does the witness know about these three months during which he was absent from the Old Town? Could he have known what the damage was before the 5th, 6th, 7th, or 15th of January? That remains unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're well conscious of that issue. Yes, Mr. Weiner. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what other damage did you notice on Od Puca Street? You mentioned the building to the left of you. What other damage?

utterances.speaker: IVO VLASICA
utterances.text: The entire street, all the shop windows were broken. Basically nothing was functional. Everything was in wooden boards. If anything did work - I cannot say whether anything was working at the time; all the shop windows were sealed off with wooden boards. There was an incredible amount of destruction. The shells or anything else that had fallen, any other kind of ordnance, had done a lot of damage. There was nothing left. Everything was broken; the doors, the windows. Then the statute of St. Joseph, it was hit. Then a shell had fallen on the Church of St. Joseph. This was done systematically. The intention was to raze the Old Town, to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is an appropriate time to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume tomorrow. Mr. Vlasica, I must ask you to return to continue with your evidence tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
